messages.content: I want to develop informative treatment-effect confidence sets when confounding proxies are weak and their conditional independence assumptions are approximately violated. The sets should have at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over explicitly quantified classes of proxy strength and assumption violations. I also want to characterize when they are strictly narrower than outcome-range-only bounds, without requiring point identification.

That sets two distinct requirements. The coverage guarantee must remain valid across the stated classes, including weak-proxy and approximate-violation cases within them. Separately, the analysis must identify when the confidence sets improve strictly on bounds obtained from the outcome range alone. Such an improvement need not reduce the effect to a single value.
What does “weak proxies” mean for this goal?

It means the proxies may provide limited information about the confounding they are meant to address. The goal does not assume that their information is strong enough for point identification. It calls for specifying the proxy-strength class quantitatively, so the coverage claim has a clear domain rather than applying only at an unspecified notion of adequate strength.
And “approximately violated” should not be read as conditional independence holding exactly?

Right. The guarantee is meant to accommodate departures from those conditional independence assumptions, within an explicitly quantified violation class. Exact independence would be a special case if that class includes it, but the stated goal is not restricted to exact independence.
Why quantify both proxy strength and the size of the assumption violation?

They describe different aspects of the problem. One concerns how much information the proxies carry; the other concerns how closely the conditional independence assumptions hold. Stating both quantitatively makes it possible to say precisely which combinations the coverage guarantee addresses. No particular measure or numerical limit for either dimension has been specified here.
Can you unpack the uniform 95% requirement?

“At least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly” means the large-sample coverage guarantee should hold over the entire specified class, not merely for each fixed case considered separately. In abstract notation, if C is the quantified class, τ(P) is the true treatment effect, and C_n is the confidence set, the intended form is liminf as n grows of inf over P in C of Pr_P{τ(P) is in C_n} being at least 0.95. That notation describes the requirement; it does not itself establish it for any proposed construction.
So showing 95% coverage separately at every fixed proxy strength might not be enough?

Correct. A pointwise asymptotic statement can leave out sequences of cases that become increasingly difficult as sample size grows. Uniform coverage asks for the at-least-95% guarantee across the explicitly stated class, including the weak-proxy and approximate-violation cases that the class admits.
Does “at least 95% asymptotic” promise 95% coverage in every finite sample?
No. It is a large-sample guarantee, and “at least” is a lower bound rather than a claim that coverage equals 95%. A finite-sample guarantee would be a different claim; it is not part of this goal.
What is being covered if the treatment effect is not point identified?

The confidence set is intended to contain the true treatment effect with the stated probability, even if the available restrictions do not single out one effect value. Lack of point identification allows multiple values to remain compatible with the information. It does not make a confidence set or a coverage requirement meaningless.
Is that the same as saying the confidence set must contain every value in an identified set?

Not automatically. Coverage of the true effect and coverage of an entire identified set are different requirements. The stated goal specifies treatment-effect confidence sets with at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage; it does not separately state an entire-identified-set coverage guarantee.
What role do the outcome-range-only bounds play?

They are the comparison baseline: bounds using the outcome range alone, without any additional narrowing attributed to the proxy information and the restrictions being considered. The goal is not merely to produce a covered set, but to characterize when that set is strictly more informative than this baseline.
Would a confidence set have to be a single number to count as more informative?

No. A set can exclude some effect values allowed by outcome-range-only bounds while still containing more than one value. That is the distinction behind “strictly narrower without requiring point identification”: genuine narrowing is possible even when a non-singleton range remains.
How should “strictly narrower” be expressed?

It needs a clear comparison criterion. If both objects are intervals, one could ask whether the confidence set has strictly smaller width under the relevant comparison, or whether it is a proper subset of the outcome-range-only interval. The characterization should say when strict improvement occurs; simply describing a set as informative would not establish that comparison.
Is strict narrowing required for every case in the class?

That is not stated. The coverage requirement is explicitly uniform over the quantified classes. The separate requirement is to characterize when strict narrowing occurs. It should not be recast as an unconditional promise that every weak-proxy and assumption-violation case yields a narrower set.
Could a method satisfy coverage but provide no improvement over outcome-range-only bounds in some cases?

The goal allows for that possibility. Coverage asks whether the true effect is included often enough; informativeness asks whether the resulting set rules out values that the baseline permits. The characterization should distinguish cases where the additional information supports strict narrowing from cases where it does not, without treating failure to narrow as a failure of coverage.
How does allowing approximate violations affect that distinction?

Permitting a larger departure from conditional independence can change which effect values remain defensible, so it matters to any claim of strict narrowing. The precise relationship cannot be asserted without the quantified violation class and the proposed confidence-set construction. The goal is to make the comparison while respecting the allowed violations, rather than obtaining narrower sets by assuming them away.
Likewise, I should not assume that a weak proxy supplies enough information to beat the baseline?

Exactly. Weak proxies are part of the setting to be addressed, not evidence by themselves that the outcome-range-only bounds can be improved. The task is to state conditions under which the proxy-based restrictions remain informative enough for strict narrowing, while preserving the coverage guarantee over the specified class.
What does “explicitly quantified classes” rule out?

It rules out leaving the scope of the guarantee at descriptions such as “reasonably strong proxies” or “small violations” with no quantitative meaning. The class must make clear which proxy strengths and which magnitudes of assumption departure are included. The current goal does not prescribe particular metrics, thresholds, or class boundaries.
Does the wording imply coverage even if proxy strength can approach zero?

Not by itself. Whether such cases are included depends on the class that is explicitly specified. If they are included, the uniform coverage claim must encompass them; if they are not, the guarantee should not be described as though it does. The stated goal does not fix that boundary in advance.
Is there also a 95% probability requirement for being narrower than the range-only bounds?

No such probability threshold is stated for narrowing. The numerical requirement is at least 95% asymptotic coverage, uniformly over the quantified classes. Strict narrowing is a separate comparison to be characterized, and its precise formulation should be made clear rather than inferred from the coverage percentage.
Then the central challenge is to keep uncertainty honest in both senses?

Yes: sampling uncertainty is reflected in the coverage requirement, and uncertainty from weak proxies and approximate conditional independence must be respected in defining the class and assessing informativeness. The intended result is a confidence set that is valid across its stated class, together with a precise account of when it excludes more effect values than outcome-range-only bounds do—even if the treatment effect remains only partially identified.

For the confidence-set goal, I propose inverting slack-adjusted Anderson–Rubin proxy moments at 95%, uniformly over conditional-independence violations with δ ≤ 0.05 and including zero-strength proxies. Then I would use positive endpoint margins to establish when the sets tighten relative to outcome-range-only bounds.

That gives the proposal two connected parts. The inversion is intended to deliver a 95% confidence set while allowing the specified assumption violations and even zero proxy strength. The endpoint-margin argument is intended to identify strict narrowing relative to the outcome-range-only baseline. Both are proposed arguments, not coverage or narrowing results already established.
Why use Anderson–Rubin-style proxy moments here?

The appeal is that a moment-inversion approach can assess candidate treatment-effect values without first relying on a precisely estimated quantity that becomes unstable as proxy strength approaches zero. In this proposal, the crucial test is whether the resulting inference actually maintains its stated coverage uniformly, including at zero strength. The name of the approach alone does not prove that property.
What does inversion mean for a confidence set?

Conceptually, one considers candidate treatment-effect values and retains those not rejected by the proposed moment-based assessment at the 95% confidence level. The collection of retained values is the confidence set. The proposal does not yet specify the exact moments, statistic, or calibration, so that description is the logic of inversion rather than a completed construction.
And why adjust the moments with slack?

The slack is meant to account for the permitted departures from conditional independence. If the moments would hold under exact assumptions but can deviate when those assumptions are approximately violated, ignoring the deviations could make the set too small for the stated coverage target. The adjustment must reflect the quantified violation class, δ ≤ 0.05, rather than quietly treating the assumptions as exact.
Does δ ≤ 0.05 tell us the precise form of the adjustment?

No. It specifies the proposed upper bound on the conditional-independence violations, but it does not by itself define the metric used to measure them or a formula translating that bound into slack for particular proxy moments. Those details would have to be explicit before the uniform coverage claim could be evaluated.
I want to be clear that the guarantee includes zero-strength proxies, not just proxies that are weak but still nonzero.

That is an important feature of the proposal. The intended uniform 95% coverage statement includes zero proxy strength, alongside the permitted violations δ ≤ 0.05. It cannot depend on imposing a positive lower bound on proxy strength while claiming to cover zero-strength cases.
Would including zero strength force every resulting confidence set to equal the outcome-range-only bounds?

Not as a blanket statement. The proposed coverage domain and the conditions for strict narrowing are different claims. At a case with zero proxy strength, the proxy moments might not supply a basis for excluding additional values; whether any narrowing remains would depend on what the specified restrictions imply. The proposal calls for characterizing tightening through positive endpoint margins, not promising it in every covered case.
How do the positive endpoint margins enter?

They are the proposed way to certify a strict gap between a confidence-set endpoint and the corresponding endpoint of the outcome-range-only bounds. For example, a positive inward margin at an endpoint would distinguish genuine narrowing from an endpoint that merely coincides with the baseline. The proposal does not give a numerical margin or establish that one is positive in any particular case.
Does tightening require moving both endpoints inward?

Not necessarily as a conceptual comparison. An inward shift at one endpoint, with no offsetting expansion elsewhere, can make an interval strictly narrower than the outcome-range-only interval. But the exact endpoint criterion for this proposal still needs to be stated carefully, especially if the confidence set need not be a single interval. What matters is that a claimed positive margin genuinely establishes strict narrowing under the chosen comparison.
So a margin should not just be an improvement in an intermediate calculation?

Right. To support the stated aim, a positive endpoint margin must translate into a stricter bound on admissible treatment-effect values than the outcome-range-only bound. A positive quantity somewhere inside a derivation would not suffice unless it yields that endpoint comparison.
Could this tightening occur without identifying one treatment effect?

Yes. If the resulting set rules out values near an outcome-range-only endpoint but still contains multiple treatment-effect values, it is strictly narrower without point identification. That is precisely the kind of distinction the endpoint-margin part of the proposal is meant to capture.
Is the 95% claim about the set containing the true effect, or about the endpoint margins being positive?

It is the proposed confidence level for coverage of the true treatment effect. Positive endpoint margins concern informativeness relative to outcome-range-only bounds. The proposal does not assign a separate 95% probability to the margins being positive.
What would the uniformity statement have to cover?

It would have to cover the explicitly stated combination of allowed conditional-independence violations, δ ≤ 0.05, and proxy strengths including zero. In particular, a coverage argument that works only when proxy strength stays away from zero, or only when δ is exactly zero, would not establish the proposed uniform claim.
Is “at 95%” a finite-sample guarantee?

The earlier goal calls for at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly over the specified classes. Reading this proposal in that context, the intended 95% property is a uniform asymptotic coverage target, not an asserted finite-sample guarantee. Establishing it still requires an argument for the particular slack-adjusted inversion.
Could the slack needed for δ ≤ 0.05 make the set less informative?

It could affect informativeness: allowing violations means candidate effects cannot be excluded merely because their moments differ by an amount the violation class permits. That is why the endpoint-margin condition matters. It would show when there is still a strict improvement over outcome-range-only bounds after accommodating the allowed departures, rather than obtaining an apparently narrow set by omitting the slack.
I do not want the narrowing claim to rely on assuming positive proxy strength if coverage includes zero strength.

The claims should be kept distinct and explicit. Uniform coverage is proposed across the class that includes zero strength. Strict narrowing is to be characterized where positive endpoint margins can be established; the proposal does not say they must arise at zero strength or throughout the entire coverage class. Stating any conditions for those margins would make that distinction transparent.
Then I should not present the Anderson–Rubin inversion as already verified to handle every δ ≤ 0.05 case?

Correct. It is a proposed route to that guarantee. Verification would require defining the conditional-independence violation measure, specifying how its δ ≤ 0.05 bound determines the moment slack, and showing that the inverted procedure attains at least 95% asymptotic coverage uniformly across the stated strength-and-violation class, including zero-strength proxies.
And for the informativeness part, the key comparison stays with outcome-range-only bounds?

Yes. The positive endpoint margins are meant to characterize when the confidence set is strictly narrower than bounds based only on the outcome range. The comparison does not require a singleton confidence set or point identification; it requires a defensible strict inward improvement while maintaining the proposed coverage standard.
When do profiled proxy moments exclude both outcome-range endpoints after δ-slack, even as proxy singular values approach zero?

The key condition would be separation at each endpoint *after* allowing both profiling and the permitted δ-slack. For an endpoint to be excluded, no admissible profiled choice and no departure allowed by the violation class should make its proxy moments sufficiently compatible with the data. To maintain that exclusion as proxy singular values approach zero, the separation must not disappear along those weak-proxy cases. Whether that happens depends on the moments and the permitted departures; it is not implied by using Anderson–Rubin-style inversion.
Can you make “after profiling and slack” more precise without assuming a particular moment formula?

Schematically, take either outcome-range endpoint as a candidate effect. Consider the smallest discrepancy its proxy moments can achieve after optimizing over whatever quantities the procedure profiles out and allowing every moment departure justified by δ-slack. Endpoint exclusion requires that this *best achievable* discrepancy still exceed the relevant testing tolerance. This is a conceptual criterion, not a specified discrepancy measure or a calculation for the proposed procedure.
Why take the smallest discrepancy rather than checking the moments at one convenient profiled value?

Because a candidate endpoint remains compatible if *any* admissible profiled choice can explain it within the allowed slack. Finding one choice with a large discrepancy would not rule out another choice with a small one. Exclusion has to survive the profiling step, rather than depend on a particular choice within it.
And the δ-slack is applied before I decide whether an endpoint is excluded?

Yes. The question is whether the endpoint conflicts with the moments even after accounting for the allowed conditional-independence violations. In the proposal discussed here, those violations have δ ≤ 0.05. An endpoint that could be excluded only by setting the violation allowance to zero has not been excluded under the proposed δ-slack analysis.
Does δ ≤ 0.05 mean I can simply subtract 0.05 from each moment discrepancy?

Not without a definition that warrants it. The number bounds the proposed violation class, but translating it into moment slack depends on how violations are measured and how they affect the moments. The endpoint comparison must use the slack justified by that translation; it cannot assume that 0.05 is automatically on the same scale as every moment.
What changes when the proxy singular values approach zero?

The proxy information represented by those weakening directions can become less able to distinguish candidate effects. The question is whether, after profiling and δ-slack, there is nevertheless enough separation to reject *each* endpoint. If every discrepancy distinguishing an endpoint shrinks away with the singular values, a fixed positive endpoint margin cannot persist on that basis alone.
So does a singular value near zero automatically prevent excluding an endpoint?

No. It signals that a particular proxy direction is weak; by itself it does not specify the entire profiled moment discrepancy at an endpoint. Exclusion could still be possible if an admissible discrepancy remains sufficiently large after slack and profiling. Equally, one cannot infer that such a discrepancy exists merely because a proposed test is robust to weak proxies.
I want to distinguish valid coverage from the ability to exclude an endpoint.

They are separate properties. Moment inversion can be designed to retain its coverage target when proxies are weak, including at zero strength, yet have little ability to exclude endpoint candidates there. Weak-proxy-robust calibration addresses the risk of erroneous exclusion; it does not guarantee useful exclusion. The endpoint question asks for an additional informativeness condition.
If a population discrepancy is positive at both endpoints, is that enough?

For a fixed case, positive post-slack, post-profiling discrepancies are the basic population-level reason exclusion might become possible as sampling uncertainty diminishes. For a claim that persists *even as singular values approach zero*, positivity only at each fixed nonzero strength may be insufficient: those discrepancies could tend to zero along a sequence of weaker proxies. A uniform narrowing claim would need separation that persists over the sequences it covers, together with suitable control of the sampling error and test threshold.
Would that mean a lower bound on the proxy singular values?

Not necessarily. A lower bound on singular values would avoid the vanishing-strength cases rather than answer the question about them. The relevant lower bound, if one seeks persistent endpoint exclusion, is on the *effective discrepancy at the endpoints after profiling and δ-slack*, expressed on an appropriate testing scale. Such a bound would have to hold despite singular values approaching zero; whether it can is an open part of this question.
What do you mean by “on an appropriate testing scale”?

A population discrepancy has to be judged against uncertainty in its estimated moments and the rule used to invert them. A raw numerical gap is not enough if its scale changes with the weakening proxies or with the profiling operation. To conclude that an endpoint is excluded with high probability, the adjusted separation must dominate the relevant sampling fluctuations and rejection threshold under the proposed calibration.
Could a discrepancy that shrinks with the singular values still exclude an endpoint?

Possibly for some sequences, if it shrinks slowly enough relative to the procedure’s uncertainty. But that is weaker than saying both endpoints remain excluded uniformly as singular values approach zero without specifying a rate. If the usable discrepancy is too small relative to sampling variation, coverage-compatible inversion may retain the endpoint. The question therefore requires attention to both the post-slack gap and its rate relative to uncertainty.
Why emphasize *both* outcome-range endpoints?

Because they are two separate candidate treatment effects. A profiled moment argument may rule out one while leaving the other compatible after slack, especially since profiling can produce different best-fitting choices at different candidates. To establish exclusion of both, the proposed criterion must hold at each endpoint rather than relying on an aggregate indication of some informativeness.
Must the same profiled choice fail at both endpoints?

No. Each endpoint should be assessed under its own most favorable admissible profiling. To exclude the lower endpoint, every admissible profiled explanation for that endpoint must leave a detectable discrepancy after slack; the analogous statement must separately hold for the upper endpoint. Requiring one common profiled choice to fail at both would not address what inversion actually allows at each candidate.
If both endpoints are rejected, can I immediately say the confidence set is strictly inside the outcome-range-only bounds?

Rejecting the two endpoint *points* is not by itself enough to guarantee a positive inward margin. The retained set might still approach an endpoint arbitrarily closely. For the proposed endpoint-margin characterization, one needs a gap that supports excluding a neighborhood at each endpoint, under appropriate continuity and uniformity conditions. Those conditions have not been established just by asking whether the endpoint points are excluded.
What would a positive endpoint margin say in this setting?

It would say that the retained treatment-effect values stay a strictly positive distance inward from an outcome-range endpoint, under the stated comparison. A positive margin at both endpoints would give a clear form of two-sided tightening relative to outcome-range-only bounds, even if the set between those margins contains multiple values. Whether the profiled proxy moments provide those margins after δ-slack is precisely what needs to be characterized.
Is excluding both endpoints required to get *any* strict improvement over outcome-range-only bounds?

No. One-sided inward narrowing could already be a strict improvement under a suitable set comparison. Your current question is stronger: it asks when the moments exclude *both* endpoints, potentially supporting margins at both ends. That stronger property should not be treated as necessary for every possible form of strict narrowing.
Could I argue from a positive gap at each endpoint to positive margins nearby?

Only with enough regularity to carry the gap into neighboring candidate effects. If the profiled, slack-adjusted discrepancy behaves continuously near an endpoint and its positive separation is robust over the relevant class, that could support a neighborhood-exclusion argument. The details matter: profiling, allowable violations, and the sampling threshold all have to be handled in that passage from a point gap to an endpoint margin.
What if the slack absorbs the entire endpoint discrepancy?

Then that discrepancy supplies no basis for excluding the endpoint under the allowed violations. Even a nonzero discrepancy computed under exact conditional independence would not help if it can be explained by departures within δ ≤ 0.05 after profiling. Another defensible source of separation would be needed; the current proposal does not assert that one exists.
And if profiling can make one endpoint fit perfectly?

Then the profiled moments cannot exclude that endpoint on the basis of a positive residual discrepancy, regardless of how large the discrepancy might be at other profiled choices. This is why the infimum over admissible choices is central to the question. It also illustrates why endpoint exclusion cannot be concluded from proxy strength or from an unprofiled calculation alone.
At zero proxy strength, should I expect the endpoint-exclusion condition to hold?

The proposal aims for coverage even at zero proxy strength; it does not promise endpoint exclusion there. If zero strength removes every moment distinction relevant to an endpoint, the requisite post-slack separation would not hold on that basis. Whether any separation remains at zero strength cannot be decided without specifying the moments and admissible class.
Does a 95% confidence procedure imply that it should reject both endpoints with 95% probability?

No. The 95% target concerns coverage of the true treatment effect, not the probability of rejecting particular endpoint candidates. Indeed, if an endpoint can be the true effect in a case covered by the guarantee, a procedure with valid coverage cannot also be required to exclude that true endpoint with probability tending to one in that case. A strong endpoint-exclusion claim needs conditions that make the endpoints incompatible with the relevant restrictions.
How would you phrase the answer to my question without claiming a result we have not proved?

Both outcome-range endpoints can be excluded by the proposed inversion when, for *each* endpoint, its proxy moments remain detectably incompatible with every admissible profiled explanation after the justified δ-slack, and that incompatibility persists on the testing scale along the weak-proxy sequences under consideration. Exclusion of neighborhoods—and thus positive margins at both endpoints—needs an additional argument carrying those gaps to nearby effects. Whether these conditions hold as proxy singular values approach zero is the question to resolve, not a consequence already established by the proposal.

Here is my hypothesis about the endpoint question: if the proxy-moment gaps at both outcome-range endpoints exceed δ plus the 95% critical radius, the confidence set strictly tightens the outcome-range-only bounds, even when the proxies are rank-deficient.

That is a proposed sufficient condition for two-sided tightening. It compares the discrepancy at each endpoint with both the allowed conditional-independence violation and the testing tolerance. Rank deficiency is not, by itself, meant to defeat the conclusion if those endpoint gaps remain. The implication still needs to be established for the profiled moments and the confidence-set construction.
Can we write the condition schematically?

Let G_L and G_U denote the relevant proxy-moment gaps at the lower and upper outcome-range endpoints, each calculated after profiling over admissible choices. In the units contemplated by the hypothesis, the condition is G_L > δ + r_95 and G_U > δ + r_95, where r_95 is the 95% critical radius. This is shorthand for the proposed comparison, not a definition of a particular moment statistic.
Why must the gaps be calculated after profiling?

An endpoint cannot be excluded just because its moments disagree at one profiled choice. If another admissible choice makes that endpoint fit within the allowed slack and critical radius, it may remain in the inverted set. The gap relevant to the hypothesis is therefore the discrepancy left at each endpoint after giving that endpoint its most favorable admissible profiling.
In that notation, is δ already subtracted from G_L and G_U?

No. As stated, the gaps are being compared with δ plus the critical radius, so δ has not already been taken out of them. Otherwise the violation allowance would be counted twice. A precise formulation would need to define the gap and the δ-slack in compatible terms; the schematic inequalities express the hypothesis’s intended separation.
How should I interpret the 95% critical radius in the comparison?

It represents the tolerance supplied by the proposed 95% calibration of the moment assessment. The endpoint gap must exceed not only the permitted assumption departure but also the amount of discrepancy that the assessment does not treat as grounds for rejection. The phrase does not, on its own, specify how that radius is calculated or prove that the resulting procedure has 95% coverage.
What does strict inequality add here?

It gives a positive excess over the combined allowance at each endpoint. Equality would not supply that positive separation. For the proposed strict tightening claim, the excess is what could support ruling out values at the ends of the outcome-range-only bounds, subject to the argument that translates endpoint gaps into inward margins.
Why require the condition at both endpoints?

Because it is a two-sided version of tightening. The lower and upper endpoints are separate candidate effects, and their best-fitting profiled choices need not coincide. A gap at only one endpoint could support one-sided improvement, but it would not establish the hypothesis that both outcome-range endpoints are excluded.
Does excluding the two exact endpoint values already establish strict tightening?

For a positive inward margin, more is needed than rejection of two isolated points: retained values must also be kept away from the endpoints. The strict excess in the hypothesis is a potential basis for that step, but one must show that the relevant gap persists for nearby candidate effects under the profiling, slack, and critical-radius comparison. Without that step, endpoint exclusion alone does not establish a positive margin.
So the proposed implication includes a neighborhood argument?

Yes, if “strict bound tightening” means moving both bounds inward by positive amounts. The endpoint inequalities identify where separation starts. A proof would need to carry it into neighborhoods of both endpoints, rather than assuming that a positive gap at a point automatically gives a gap throughout a neighborhood.
How can the hypothesis allow rank-deficient proxies?

Rank deficiency says some proxy directions do not provide independent identifying information. It does not, by itself, say that the profiled proxy-moment gap at either outcome-range endpoint is zero. The hypothesis is conditional: even with rank deficiency, if both endpoint gaps exceed δ plus the 95% critical radius, those gaps are proposed to support strict tightening. It does not assert that rank-deficient proxies generally produce such gaps.
Would an arbitrarily small positive singular value be handled the same way?

The intended comparison is still about the post-profiling endpoint gaps, rather than a minimum singular-value requirement. As singular values approach zero, the relevant question is whether both gaps continue to exceed the combined allowance on the testing scale. Their doing so is not guaranteed merely by being positive at some stronger proxy configuration.
Is the endpoint-gap hypothesis another way of requiring point identification?

No. It requires the two outcome-range endpoints to be incompatible with the profiled moments beyond the permitted slack and critical radius. Values between the resulting inward bounds may still remain admissible. The proposed conclusion is strict improvement on outcome-range-only bounds, not identification of one treatment-effect value.
What if the gap at one endpoint exceeds the threshold and the other does not?

Then the stated two-endpoint sufficient condition is not met. There may still be a basis for a one-sided improvement, but that would be a different, weaker conclusion. The hypothesis specifically connects gaps exceeding δ plus the 95% critical radius at *both* endpoints to strict tightening at both ends.
What if both gaps exceed δ, but neither exceeds δ plus the critical radius?

They would exceed the assumed violation allowance but not the full threshold in the hypothesis. That would not meet the proposed condition for excluding the endpoints through the 95% moment assessment. Accounting for sampling uncertainty is part of why the critical radius appears in addition to δ.
Should I say this condition proves the 95% uniform coverage guarantee too?

No. The gap condition concerns when the set is informative relative to outcome-range-only bounds. The at-least-95% uniform asymptotic coverage target is a separate requirement for the slack-adjusted inversion, including the proposed class with δ ≤ 0.05 and zero-strength proxies. Endpoint separation does not substitute for a coverage argument.
And uniform coverage does not establish these gaps?

Correct. A procedure might cover the true effect at the required rate yet retain one or both outcome-range endpoints. Coverage constrains erroneous exclusions; it does not supply the positive endpoint discrepancies needed for tightening. That is why the hypothesis states an additional condition.
Does rank deficiency change how the 95% critical radius should be chosen?

The hypothesis does not specify a calibration rule, so it cannot settle that question. Whatever radius the proposed procedure uses must support its intended coverage over the stated proxy-strength class, including rank-deficient or zero-strength cases as applicable. The endpoint-gap comparison must then use that valid radius, rather than one justified only away from rank deficiency.
Am I claiming tightening at every rank-deficient case?

No. “Even with rank-deficient proxies” means rank deficiency is not an automatic barrier *when the two gap inequalities hold*. It does not assert that those inequalities hold for all rank-deficient proxies, or that the set always improves on outcome-range-only bounds at zero strength.
What is the most careful way to state the hypothesis in one sentence?

A careful version is: If the profiled proxy-moment gap at each outcome-range endpoint exceeds the justified δ-slack plus the valid 95% critical radius, and that separation yields positive inward endpoint margins, then the resulting confidence set is hypothesized to tighten the outcome-range-only bounds at both ends, potentially even with rank-deficient proxies.
My plan is to derive a uniformly calibrated 95% inversion and compute profiled endpoint margins across proxy strengths 0–0.2 and conditional-independence violations δ ≤ 0.05.

That plan addresses both parts of the endpoint question. The inversion is meant to retain the 95% coverage target across the stated strength-and-violation class, including proxy strength zero. The margin calculations are meant to show, for each case considered, whether the profiled proxy moments leave a positive inward gap at either outcome-range endpoint after the permitted violations are accounted for. Neither the calibration nor the margins have been derived yet.
What does “uniformly calibrated” require in this plan?

The proposed 95% inversion must meet the earlier goal of at least 95% asymptotic coverage over the whole specified class, rather than only at each fixed positive proxy strength. The range 0–0.2 includes zero, and the violation allowance extends through δ ≤ 0.05. Calibration that relies on proxies staying bounded away from zero, or on exact conditional independence, would not establish that intended claim.
Is the 0–0.2 range a range for the treatment effect?

No. It is the planned range of proxy strengths. The treatment-effect candidates belong to the confidence-set inversion, and the outcome-range endpoints are the bounds against which tightening will be assessed. The plan does not specify numerical treatment-effect endpoints.
Does specifying 0–0.2 tell us exactly how proxy strength is measured?

Not yet. It specifies the range to be covered, but a derivation would still need to define the proxy-strength measure to which those numbers apply. That definition matters for stating a verifiable uniform claim and for interpreting margin calculations as strength approaches zero.
How does δ ≤ 0.05 enter the calibration?

The inversion must allow the conditional-independence departures admitted by that violation class. That means the moment assessment cannot treat every deviation from an exact-independence moment restriction as evidence against a candidate treatment effect. The derivation still needs to specify how δ measures a violation and how its bound becomes justified slack in the proxy moments; the number 0.05 alone does not supply that translation.
Is the 95% part a critical-radius choice or the coverage guarantee?

The target is a 95% confidence-set inversion with at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage. A critical radius may be part of how the inversion is calibrated, but choosing something called a “95% radius” is not enough by itself. The derivation must show that the resulting acceptance rule has the intended coverage throughout proxy strengths 0–0.2 and violations δ ≤ 0.05.
What would I be computing for each endpoint?

For each outcome-range endpoint, the planned margin is the distance by which the confidence-set bound can be placed inward relative to that endpoint, using the profiled, slack-adjusted proxy-moment assessment. Profiling matters because each candidate endpoint must be given its best admissible fit. A positive margin would express strict inward tightening at that endpoint; a margin that is not positive would not establish it.
Would I use one profiled choice for both endpoints?

The two endpoints should be assessed separately. Profiling asks whether each endpoint has an admissible explanation, and its most favorable explanation need not be the same as the other endpoint’s. Computing a margin for each endpoint avoids inferring two-sided tightening from a calculation that addresses only one candidate.
How does computing margins answer the question about singular values approaching zero?

The strength range includes values down to zero. Examining the profiled endpoint margins across that range can reveal whether any claimed inward separation persists as proxies weaken, rather than being visible only at stronger values. To turn that observation into a uniform conclusion near zero, the derivation must also account for how the moments, slack, and 95% calibration behave along weakening-proxy cases. The plan does not presume that the margins stay positive.
Does the plan require positive margins throughout the entire 0–0.2 range?

No. It requires computing and characterizing the margins across that range. Uniform 95% coverage is the intended guarantee across the class; strict tightening is a separate property that may hold only under additional endpoint-separation conditions. The calculations should make clear where margins are positive, rather than assume positivity at every strength.
And δ ≤ 0.05 applies to the margin calculations as well as to coverage?
