Would the theorem require point identification to work?

No point-identification requirement is stated. A confidence set can retain multiple treatment-effect values while meeting the at-least-95% uniform asymptotic coverage guarantee. This result concerns validity of the set, not whether it reduces to a singleton.
Can I state that every zero-strength confidence set excludes both outcome-range endpoints?

No. Including zero strength in the coverage class ensures the coverage claim applies there under the other conditions; it does not ensure endpoint exclusion. A procedure can be valid at zero strength even when its confidence set is wide.
What if someone reads “worst-case” as meaning the theorem applies to every imaginable moment configuration?

The theorem’s scope is the explicitly stated class, not every configuration. Regardless of how the critical values are motivated, the coverage result requires bounded, nondegenerate moments, |bridge| ≤ 5, strengths 0–0.2, and δ ≤ 0.05. “Worst-case” should be understood relative to that class, not as permission to drop its conditions.
What is the careful distinction between the coverage theorem and a simulated coverage figure?

The theorem establishes an asymptotic lower bound uniformly over its stated class. A simulated coverage figure estimates performance for the cases and sample size evaluated in a simulation. The two can be discussed together, but a simulation estimate is not the proof, and the theorem is not a claim that every finite-sample estimate must equal or exceed 95%.
Could the moment assumptions be left implicit because they sound technical?

They should remain explicit in any claim of proved coverage. Saying only that Gaussian-max calibration works for strengths 0–0.2 and δ ≤ 0.05 would omit the boundedness and nondegeneracy conditions under which the result is stated. You can keep their description brief without dropping them.
Does the proof establish anything for proxy strengths greater than 0.2?
The stated guarantee covers strengths from 0 to 0.2. It does not assert a result above 0.2. That limit describes the scope of this proof, not a claim that inference necessarily fails outside it.
How would you state the result in one sentence without overselling it?

With |bridge| ≤ 5 and bounded, nondegenerate moments, Gaussian-max calibration yields treatment-effect confidence sets with at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage over proxy strengths 0–0.2 and conditional-independence violations δ ≤ 0.05.
Can auxiliary validation data justify |bridge| ≤ 5 when proxies have zero strength, while preserving the uniform 95% coverage guarantee?

Potentially, but that cannot be concluded without specifying what the validation data reveal about the bridge. They would need to justify the bound for the relevant zero-strength cases, not merely make it seem plausible. Coverage would then have to be assessed under the restriction as justified—or account for uncertainty if the restriction is inferred from data.
Why is zero proxy strength particularly important to this question?

At zero strength, the proxies themselves may offer no leverage for constraining the bridge. Auxiliary validation information could, in principle, provide a different basis for doing so. But zero strength does not tell us whether such information is available or whether it identifies a bound of 5. That depends on what the validation data measure and the assumptions connecting them to the bridge.
Would observing validation data be enough to say |bridge| ≤ 5?

No. Data alone do not turn an uncertain bound into a known restriction. You would need an argument linking the validation observations to the same bridge that appears in the confidence-set analysis, including an account of sampling uncertainty and any assumptions required for that link.
What would it mean for the validation data to justify the bound rather than merely suggest it?

They would have to support a defensible statement that the relevant bridge satisfies |bridge| ≤ 5, with the scope and uncertainty of that statement made explicit. A sample estimate whose magnitude happens to be below 5 would not establish that the underlying bridge lies below 5. Nor would information about a different quantity establish the restriction without a justified connection.
Could I simply apply the existing 95% calibration after checking the bridge bound in validation data?

That depends on what “checking” establishes. If |bridge| ≤ 5 is genuinely justified as a condition defining the covered class, the stated coverage result can be invoked for cases satisfying its other conditions. If the check can mistakenly accept the restriction, applying a calibration conditional on the restriction does not automatically retain 95% coverage across cases where the restriction may be false.
Is a separate validation sample automatically enough to remove that problem?

No. Separation can help with how data-dependent decisions are analyzed, but it cannot make an uncertain bound certain. Even with separate data, the possibility of incorrectly concluding |bridge| ≤ 5 has to be included in any coverage claim that relies on the conclusion.
What exactly could go wrong if the validation data sometimes certify a false bound?

In those cases, the resulting confidence set is being used outside the bridge class for which the 95% guarantee is stated. The guarantee for |bridge| ≤ 5 does not itself bound coverage when the actual bridge exceeds 5. A uniform claim over a broader class therefore needs control of that certification error as well as control of the confidence-set inversion.
Can you illustrate the accounting without proposing a particular validation method?

Suppose, purely schematically, that a validation procedure can incorrectly certify the bridge restriction with probability at most α_v uniformly over the class at issue, and the subsequent confidence procedure misses the true effect with probability at most α_i when its restriction applies. An appropriate joint argument could then bound the total error by α_v + α_i. To guarantee at least 95% coverage through that route, the sum would need to be at most 0.05. Those error bounds and their uniformity would have to be established; none are specified for the auxiliary data in this question.
If the inversion already has a 95% guarantee under |bridge| ≤ 5, can I assign some additional positive error probability to validation and still claim at least 95% overall?

Not from a simple addition-of-errors argument. A 95% guarantee allows up to 5% noncoverage under its stated conditions; an additional possibility of wrongly certifying those conditions could push the bound beyond 5%. Preserving the overall at-least-95% claim would require a sharper joint argument or calibration that accounts for validation uncertainty, rather than just appending a fallible check.
Could validation give an interval for the bridge instead of a yes-or-no certification?

Conceptually, yes. An uncertainty set for the bridge could be carried into the treatment-effect inversion instead of treating |bridge| ≤ 5 as known. To claim uniform 95% coverage, the combined construction would need its own calibration and proof. The question does not specify such an uncertainty set or establish that it would lie within −5 to 5.
What if the validation interval crosses 5 or −5?

Then it would not, by itself, justify the fixed restriction |bridge| ≤ 5. One could not describe the bound as established merely because some values in the interval satisfy it. How to proceed would depend on a separately specified inference rule; this question does not choose one.
Does the bridge have to mean the same thing in the validation analysis and the zero-strength proxy analysis?

Yes. The validation evidence must bear on the bridge constrained by the confidence-set procedure in the cases to which the bound is applied. If that connection requires assumptions about how the validation setting relates to the target setting, those assumptions belong in the justification. No such connection has been supplied here.
Could validation information establish the restriction only at positive proxy strengths and still answer my question?

No. The question asks about zero-strength proxies. An argument confined to positive strengths would leave the boundary case unresolved. To use |bridge| ≤ 5 at zero strength, its justification must cover that case, or a uniformly valid argument must explain why the validation information extends to it.
Does the uniform guarantee need to account for how validation behaves as strengths approach zero, not only at exactly zero?

If the claim remains uniform over proxy strengths 0–0.2, yes. Validation-based justification and the resulting procedure cannot be valid only at one selected strength while being described as uniform over the full range. This includes admissible sequences approaching zero, subject to the stated conditions of the coverage result.
What other conditions should remain visible if the bridge restriction is justified?

The stated uniform asymptotic coverage result also requires bounded, nondegenerate moments, permits conditional-independence violations only through δ ≤ 0.05, and covers proxy strengths 0–0.2. Validation evidence for |bridge| ≤ 5 would address that bridge condition; it would not, on its own, establish the moment conditions or enlarge the other ranges.
If validation data justify |bridge| ≤ 5 only for some cases, can I still call the guarantee uniform?

Only with the class described accurately. Uniform coverage can be claimed over a class in which the bridge restriction and the other conditions hold. It cannot be extended to cases outside the justified class merely because some validated cases meet the restriction. If membership is itself inferred with uncertainty, that uncertainty must be incorporated into the coverage argument.
Would validation evidence that the bridge is finite be enough?

Not necessarily. The restriction in question is the numerical bound |bridge| ≤ 5. Knowing only that a bridge is finite leaves open values larger than 5 in absolute magnitude, for which the stated bridge condition does not hold.
Could the validation data instead justify a bound different from 5?

They might, in principle, support some bound, but that would not automatically establish the guarantee stated for |bridge| ≤ 5 or justify substituting a different number into its proof. This question is specifically whether the data can justify 5 while preserving the stated uniform coverage claim; no validation result or alternative bound is supplied.
Does justification of |bridge| ≤ 5 guarantee strict tightening at zero strength?

No. It addresses whether the restriction used by the confidence-set analysis is warranted. Strict tightening remains a separate question about the profiled moment gaps and the resulting bounds. A valid bridge restriction does not force both endpoint gaps to exceed δ plus the critical radius in every zero-strength case.
What can I answer now, before seeing any description of the auxiliary validation data?

The answer is conditional: auxiliary validation data could justify |bridge| ≤ 5 at zero proxy strength if they provide defensible information about the relevant bridge at that strength. Preserving at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage would additionally require that any uncertainty in imposing the restriction be included in a valid joint calibration or proof, while retaining the bounded, nondegenerate moment conditions, strengths 0–0.2, and δ ≤ 0.05. Without the validation data and their connection to the bridge, neither justification nor preservation of the guarantee has been established.

My hypothesis is that independent validation data certifying a bridge norm of at most 5 at 97.5% confidence would allow a 97.5% Anderson–Rubin (AR) inversion to achieve at least 95% coverage, including when proxy strength is zero.

That is a proposed way to account for two sources of error: incorrectly certifying the bridge bound and excluding the true treatment effect in the AR inversion. If each error can be controlled at 2.5% over the class of interest, their combined probability can be bounded by 5%. The hypothesis needs a precise certification rule, a coverage argument for the 97.5% inversion, and a rule for what happens when certification fails.
Why use 97.5% for each part rather than 95%?

A 97.5% confidence level corresponds to a 2.5% error allowance. Allocating at most 2.5% to erroneous certification and at most 2.5% to AR noncoverage leaves a combined allowance of at most 5%, yielding the proposed at-least-95% coverage bound. Using a full 5% error allowance for each part would not give that conclusion by simple addition.
Does calling the validation data independent establish that error calculation?

No. Independence does not establish either component’s 2.5% error bound. Once suitable bounds exist, a union-bound calculation can combine them without independence. Independence may help justify how the validation-based decision and the AR assessment interact, but its precise role depends on the construction.
What would it mean to certify the bridge norm at 97.5% confidence?

It needs a rule with a controlled probability of falsely declaring the norm to be at most 5 when it is actually greater than 5. As a general illustration, one might certify only when a valid one-sided 97.5% upper confidence limit for the norm is at most 5. That illustrates the required logic, not a specified validation procedure or an established property of the available data.
Would a bridge-norm estimate below 5 be a certificate?

Not by itself. An estimate below 5 can occur even when the true norm exceeds 5. The 97.5% qualification concerns the error of the certification procedure, including its uncertainty, rather than merely the numerical value of an estimate.
Is the bridge norm necessarily the same as the earlier condition |bridge| ≤ 5?

That needs to be made explicit. If the bridge is scalar and the proposed norm is absolute value, the statements coincide. For a more general bridge, “norm ≤ 5” requires a definition of the norm and an argument that it supplies the bound needed by the AR inversion. The hypothesis should not assume those are interchangeable without specifying the connection.
How do the two error events combine?

The intended reasoning is that a missed true effect could arise from relying on a false certification, or from AR noncoverage when the restriction used by the inversion is justified. If the first event has probability at most 0.025 and the second is controlled at 0.025, a joint argument can give a total bound of 0.05. The exact event decomposition must also cover whatever the procedure does when validation does not certify the norm bound.
Why does the no-certificate case matter if my question is about certified bridges?

Because an unconditional 95% coverage claim concerns the procedure’s output across possible validation outcomes. If the procedure still returns a confidence set when certification fails, that branch must not introduce uncontrolled noncoverage. Alternatively, a claim explicitly conditional on certification would need its own justification; it does not follow simply from the two nominal 97.5% levels.
Could I just report coverage conditional on getting a certificate?

You could investigate that quantity, but it is not automatically at least 95%. A 97.5% confidence certificate controls a repeated-sampling error event; it does not mean that, among all datasets on which certification succeeds, there is automatically a 97.5% probability that the bound is true. Conditioning on the certification event requires care.
If the true bridge norm is greater than 5, could the overall procedure still have the proposed coverage?

Potentially, if false certification is sufficiently rare and the procedure handles noncertification in a coverage-preserving way. The bounded-bridge AR claim alone would not cover a true norm greater than 5. The validation-based construction would need to control the chance of incorrectly applying that bounded-bridge inversion and account for its other branch.
If the true norm is at most 5, what does validation add?

In that case the bridge restriction is true, but validation may still fail to certify it. The proposed construction must specify how that outcome is handled. The 97.5% AR inversion addresses coverage when applied under its conditions; validation supplies an evidential route for deciding whether invoking the bridge bound is warranted, not a guarantee that certification always succeeds.
Does the 97.5% AR inversion have to be valid at zero proxy strength specifically?

Yes. Including zero-strength proxies in the proposed at-least-95% result requires the AR component’s error bound to hold there under its other stated conditions. Validation of the bridge norm cannot repair a calibration that fails simply because proxy strength is zero.
And must the validation certificate itself work at zero strength?

Yes, if it is being used to justify the bridge bound in those cases. Independent validation data might contain information unavailable from zero-strength proxies, but the hypothesis does not establish that they do. The certificate’s claimed error control must apply to the relevant zero-strength cases rather than being inferred from positive-strength ones.
Can I state the at-least-95% result uniformly over the proxy-strength and violation class?

Only if both the validation error bound and the AR noncoverage bound—and the rule combining them—are uniform over the class being claimed. Pointwise 97.5% statements may be insufficient for a uniform 95% conclusion, particularly along cases whose proxy strength approaches zero. The hypothesis proposes the result but does not by itself provide those uniform arguments.
Should approximate conditional-independence violations still enter the AR stage?

Yes. A bridge certificate addresses the bridge bound, not whether conditional independence holds exactly. If the intended coverage class continues to allow violations δ ≤ 0.05, the 97.5% AR inversion must retain appropriate slack and calibration for those violations. Validation of one restriction should not silently remove the other source of uncertainty.
Do the bounded, nondegenerate moment conditions disappear once I have validation data?

No. Certifying a bridge norm does not establish moment boundedness or nondegeneracy. Any coverage argument that relies on those conditions must keep them in its stated scope, including in zero-strength cases. The hypothesis does not say that validation replaces the conditions needed for AR calibration.
Does the arithmetic give exactly 95% coverage?

It gives a proposed lower bound of at least 95% if the relevant error probabilities are each bounded as required and the procedure’s branches are accounted for. Actual coverage could be higher. In an asymptotic formulation, any approximation errors would also need to be controlled uniformly so that the limiting lower bound remains at least 95%.
Is a 97.5% AR confidence set necessarily the same width as the earlier 95% inversion?

No width comparison is established by the hypothesis. The AR confidence level, the validation decision, and the resulting set construction can all matter for informativeness. The proposed at-least-95% coverage claim should not be presented as proof that the final set is strictly narrower than outcome-range-only bounds.
So the validation argument would not itself ensure endpoint tightening at zero strength?

Correct. It would aim to justify using a bridge-norm restriction while preserving coverage. Whether the resulting confidence set excludes outcome-range endpoints or has positive inward margins remains a separate question about the profiled moments and the set produced under that restriction.
What is the most careful short statement of the hypothesis?

The hypothesis is that independent validation can certify a bridge norm ≤ 5 with uniformly controlled 2.5% false-certification error, and that a suitably calibrated 97.5% AR inversion, together with a coverage-preserving response to noncertification, then yields at least 95% coverage including zero-strength proxies. Those error controls and the combined coverage conclusion remain to be established.

I’d like to explore a different route: use LP-relaxed latent mixtures that allow proxy-independence violations δ ≤ 0.05, combine them with simultaneous 95% multinomial bands, and use dual bounds to certify narrowing relative to outcome-range-only bounds without inverting tests.

That is a proposed optimization-based route to treatment-effect confidence sets. The latent-mixture LP relaxation would describe effects compatible with the proxy restrictions and allowed violations; the simultaneous multinomial bands would account for sampling uncertainty; and dual bounds would provide a way to certify strict narrowing. Those ingredients outline the approach, but their validity and informativeness still need to be established.
What is the role of the latent mixtures?

They provide a way to represent unobserved components relevant to the treatment-effect restrictions while linking them to observable quantities. The proposed linear-programming relaxation would optimize over admissible mixtures rather than presume that one mixture, or one treatment effect, is uniquely determined. The proposal does not specify the mixture components or their constraints.
Does “LP-relaxed” mean that every solution of the linear program corresponds to a genuine latent-mixture model?

Not necessarily. A relaxation can admit additional solutions beyond those of the underlying model. For coverage, the essential direction is that the relaxation not exclude admissible true cases. Extra solutions can make the resulting set wider; they cannot be silently described as genuinely feasible latent models without a separate equivalence argument.
Why permit proxy-independence violations rather than impose independence exactly?

The proposal explicitly permits departures from the proxy-independence assumptions up to δ ≤ 0.05. Any LP constraints relying on those assumptions must allow the departures as quantified. An LP that enforces exact independence while claiming coverage for δ ≤ 0.05 would not implement the stated proposal.
Can I just add 0.05 to each LP constraint?

Not from the proposal alone. It specifies the bound δ ≤ 0.05 but not the measure of proxy-independence violation or its translation into each constraint. That translation must be justified on the scale of the quantities constrained by the LP; 0.05 is not automatically the right slack for every constraint.
What are the simultaneous 95% multinomial bands doing?

They would enclose the relevant observable multinomial probabilities jointly at the stated confidence level. The LP could then allow observable probabilities within those bands instead of treating estimated cell probabilities as exact. Simultaneity matters because the optimization may draw on several probabilities at once; separate nominal 95% intervals for each would not automatically provide 95% joint containment.
Does the 95% figure attach to the bands or to the final treatment-effect set?

The proposal specifies simultaneous 95% multinomial bands. To transfer their coverage to a treatment-effect confidence set, one must show that whenever the bands contain the true observable probabilities, the δ-relaxed LP retains the true effect under the model’s stated conditions. That containment argument, together with the bands’ calibration, would support the final coverage claim; the label on the bands alone does not prove it.
Could you explain that containment logic without choosing a particular LP?

Conceptually, consider the event on which all relevant true multinomial probabilities fall inside their simultaneous bands. If the true latent-mixture representation and its permitted proxy-independence departures are feasible for the relaxed constraints on that event, then the true treatment effect must lie between the LP’s admissible effect extremes. Thus, band containment can imply effect-set containment. Whether the implication holds depends on how the actual relaxation is specified.
Would the LP simply use each band’s midpoint?

That would not generally retain the simultaneous-band uncertainty. The proposed confidence-set logic allows the observable probabilities to vary within the bands, subject to the other constraints. Substituting only midpoints could exclude the true probabilities even on the event that the bands cover them.
Why call the result a confidence set if the LP may have many feasible mixtures?

The set concerns treatment-effect values, not a unique mixture. Optimizing the effect over all admissible mixtures and observable probabilities produces an outer range of compatible effect values. That range can cover the true effect while remaining non-singleton, which fits the goal of informative confidence sets without requiring point identification.
What does “without inversion” mean here?

It means the proposed narrowing certificate comes from optimization and its dual bounds, rather than testing each candidate treatment effect and inverting those tests. The method still has to account for uncertainty through the simultaneous bands. “Without inversion” is a distinction in construction, not a waiver of the coverage requirement.
How would the dual bounds certify narrowing?

In an LP formulation, a valid dual bound can certify that the maximum feasible treatment effect falls strictly below the outcome-range-only upper endpoint, or that the minimum feasible effect lies strictly above its lower endpoint. Comparing certified effect extrema with the baseline endpoints would establish an inward gap. The proposal supplies neither a dual solution nor a numerical gap, so it does not yet assert that such a certificate exists.
Would one dual certificate suffice for both endpoints?

The lower and upper extremes are separate optimization questions. A certificate addressing the upper extreme alone would not establish a positive lower-endpoint margin, and vice versa. For two-sided narrowing, both comparisons need support; a one-sided certificate could still show a more limited strict improvement.
Is dual feasibility enough even if we have not identified the mixture?

A valid dual bound can bound an LP optimum without selecting a unique primal mixture. That is why dual certification is compatible with partial identification. Its interpretation still depends on the LP being an appropriate outer relaxation and on the certificate applying to the band-and-δ constraints actually used.
Could a dual bound prove a narrower interval just because the LP is a relaxation?

No. Relaxing constraints typically permits more candidates, so it can weaken rather than create narrowing. A strict dual comparison would have to show that, even with the allowed relaxation, violation slack, and multinomial-band uncertainty, an outcome-range endpoint is beyond the relevant feasible effect extreme.
What if the dual bound equals the outcome-range-only endpoint?

Equality gives no strict inward gap at that endpoint. It may still be a valid bound, but it does not certify strict narrowing there. A positive separation from the baseline endpoint is needed for that particular certificate to demonstrate an improvement.
Does the proposal promise strict narrowing when proxy strength is zero?

No. Weak proxies motivate the overarching goal, but this proposal does not state which proxy-strength class its LP analysis covers or assert narrowing at zero strength. A relaxation might remain valid with very weak proxies and still return outcome-range-only bounds. Any claim about zero-strength coverage or strict narrowing needs its own explicit conditions and argument.
To meet the larger coverage goal, would we need more than simultaneous 95% bands?

Yes. We would need the bands’ required coverage uniformly over an explicitly quantified class and a uniform containment argument for the LP relaxation across that class. In particular, the proxy-strength range and the meaning of δ ≤ 0.05 would need to be stated for this approach. The present proposal specifies the violation bound and the bands, but not a proxy-strength range or a completed uniform-coverage proof.
Can a simultaneous 95% band be used to claim finite-sample 95% coverage for the effect?

Only if the band itself has that finite-sample joint guarantee and the LP containment implication holds under all relevant conditions. “Simultaneous 95% multinomial bands” does not state whether their calibration is finite-sample or asymptotic. The larger goal calls for at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage, which still requires an appropriate proof for this construction.
Does allowing δ ≤ 0.05 also affect the dual certificate?

Yes. The dual must bound the LP that actually allows the stated proxy-independence violations. A certificate for exact-independence constraints could appear sharper but would not, without further justification, certify narrowing for the δ ≤ 0.05 relaxation.
What if the simultaneous bands are wide?

Then the LP may admit more observable probabilities and, consequently, more treatment-effect values. The dual bounds might not show any inward gap relative to the outcome-range-only endpoints. The proposal seeks to characterize when a gap remains despite both sampling uncertainty and permitted assumption violations; it does not guarantee one.
Would strict narrowing mean point identification in this LP approach?

No. The LP could certify an upper bound below the outcome-range-only upper endpoint, a lower bound above its lower endpoint, or both, while leaving an interval of feasible effect values. Strict improvement over range-only bounds is distinct from narrowing to a single treatment effect.
How should we keep the dual result separate from the coverage result?

The band-and-relaxation containment argument addresses whether the true effect stays inside the confidence set at the intended rate. The dual certificate addresses whether that set excludes values the outcome range alone permits. A sound certificate of narrowing cannot replace a coverage proof, and a sound coverage proof cannot guarantee a strict dual gap.
What is the careful one-sentence description of this route?

The proposal is to form treatment-effect confidence sets from LP-relaxed latent mixtures allowing proxy-independence violations δ ≤ 0.05 and simultaneous 95% multinomial bands, then use valid dual bounds to certify strict narrowing relative to outcome-range-only bounds where possible, without test inversion or a point-identification requirement.

For the LP-relaxed latent-mixture approach, my plan is to calibrate simultaneous 95% multinomial bands, establish uniform coverage for the resulting treatment-effect sets over proxy strengths 0–0.2 and proxy-independence violations δ ≤ 0.05, and derive dual conditions for strict tightening relative to outcome-range-only bounds.

That plan separates validity from informativeness. The bands address uncertainty in the observed multinomial probabilities; the LP coverage argument must show that the true treatment effect remains feasible whenever those probabilities are covered, uniformly across the stated strength and violation class. The dual conditions would then identify when the resulting effect bounds move strictly inward from outcome-range-only bounds. These are planned derivations, not results already established.
What should “calibrate simultaneous 95% multinomial bands” accomplish?

The bands should contain all the relevant true multinomial probabilities together at the intended 95% level. Simultaneity matters because the LP can use several probabilities at once. Giving each probability its own nominal 95% interval would not, by itself, establish 95% joint coverage.
Is band coverage the same claim as coverage of the treatment-effect set?

No. Band coverage concerns the observable probabilities. Treatment-effect coverage additionally requires a containment argument: when the bands contain the true probabilities, the δ-relaxed latent-mixture LP must allow the true effect under the stated assumptions. The planned proof needs both steps.
Why describe the LP as a relaxation in that argument?

The relaxation may admit more latent mixtures or effect values than the underlying restrictions require. For coverage, the important direction is that it must not omit a true admissible representation. Permitting extra values may reduce precision, but excluding the true representation would break the proposed route from band coverage to effect coverage.
Does δ ≤ 0.05 have to enter the LP feasibility argument explicitly?

Yes. The coverage class permits proxy-independence violations through δ=0.05. The LP constraints must accommodate those permitted departures, and the proof must show feasibility for admissible cases throughout that class. An argument that works only under exact proxy independence would not establish this plan’s stated coverage scope.
Can I treat 0.05 as a generic amount of slack in every multinomial constraint?

Not without defining how δ measures the proxy-independence violation and how that measure limits each relevant constraint. The number 0.05 states the allowed magnitude in the proposed class; a justified translation is needed before it becomes LP slack on any particular scale.
What does the proxy-strength range add to the coverage claim?

It makes the proposed class explicit: proxy strengths run from 0 through 0.2. Establishing coverage uniformly over that range includes zero-strength cases and cases approaching zero. The plan cannot rely on an unstated positive lower bound on proxy strength while claiming coverage over 0–0.2.
Is 0–0.2 a range of treatment effects or a range of multinomial probabilities?

Neither. It is the planned proxy-strength range. The violation allowance is separately δ ≤ 0.05, and the treatment-effect bounds are outputs of the LP. The plan does not specify numerical treatment-effect endpoints.
Could pointwise coverage at each fixed strength in that range satisfy the plan?

Not necessarily. Uniform coverage must control the least favorable admissible cases over the stated class as sample size grows, including cases whose strength approaches zero with sample size. Separate fixed-strength asymptotic claims need not provide that control.
Can you state the intended uniform claim without presuming it has been proved?

If C_n denotes the LP-based treatment-effect set and τ(P) the true effect, the planned claim is that the limit inferior, as sample size grows, of the infimum of Pr_P{τ(P) ∈ C_n} over the specified strength-and-violation class is at least 0.95. That is a statement to establish using the calibrated bands and LP containment, not something guaranteed just by writing it down.
Does calibrating bands at 95% automatically make their coverage uniform over proxy strengths 0–0.2?

No. The nominal level and the uniformity of its justification are different matters. The plan requires calibration suitable for the specified class, including its weak-proxy boundary, and then a uniform argument carrying joint band containment through the LP to effect containment.
What should happen conceptually on the event that the simultaneous bands contain the true multinomial probabilities?

On that event, the LP should permit the true observable probabilities and at least one admissible latent-mixture representation consistent with the allowed δ violation. If the true treatment effect is attainable through that feasible representation, it lies within the LP-derived effect set. The plan is to demonstrate this implication for the stated class; it is not established by the bands alone.
Do I need to identify which latent mixture is the true one?

No. A coverage argument needs to establish that a true admissible representation is included, not recover it uniquely. The resulting treatment-effect set can contain multiple values. That is compatible with both LP relaxation and the aim of obtaining useful bounds without point identification.
Could I calibrate the bands using one proxy strength and reuse them throughout 0–0.2?

Only if a uniform argument justifies doing so. Calibration at one selected strength does not by itself control joint band coverage—or resulting effect coverage—over all strengths from 0 to 0.2. The plan specifies the full range as the domain of the intended guarantee.
Does the same issue arise across δ values?

Yes. The LP containment argument must cover the permitted proxy-independence violations throughout δ ≤ 0.05, including the boundary. A proof restricted to δ=0 would leave out the approximate-violation cases in the plan.
What are the dual conditions supposed to characterize?

They are meant to characterize when the LP-based confidence set is strictly narrower than bounds using the outcome range alone. A dual bound could certify that the greatest feasible effect falls below the range-only upper endpoint, that the least feasible effect rises above the range-only lower endpoint, or both. The plan is to derive conditions under which such strict comparisons hold; no particular certificate or margin has been supplied.
Would a dual certificate need to use the same uncertainty allowances as the coverage set?

Yes. To certify narrowing of the proposed confidence set, a dual bound must apply to the LP with the simultaneous multinomial bands and the allowed δ ≤ 0.05 violations in place. A sharper bound obtained by dropping band uncertainty or imposing exact independence would address a different set.
Why use a dual bound rather than just look at an LP solution?

The proposed dual conditions offer a way to certify an extreme feasible effect relative to an outcome-range endpoint. A feasible example on its own shows that one value can occur; it does not generally show that no more extreme value is feasible. A valid bound on the optimum is what supports a strict comparison with the baseline.
Does a dual condition for the upper endpoint also prove tightening at the lower endpoint?

No. The upper and lower effect extremes are distinct comparisons. A strict upper certificate establishes an upper-side improvement; a lower-side improvement requires its own supporting bound. The planned characterization should distinguish one-sided from two-sided tightening rather than infer both from one certificate.
How strict must a comparison be to count as tightening?

It needs a positive inward difference from the corresponding outcome-range-only bound. Equality can provide a valid bound but not strict tightening at that end. If the plan aims to establish positive margins, the dual conditions must support an actual gap, not merely exclude a single endpoint while allowing values arbitrarily close to it.
Would the dual conditions guarantee tightening for every strength from 0 to 0.2?

That is not stated. Coverage is the property to establish uniformly across the full strength-and-violation class. The dual analysis is to characterize *when* strict tightening occurs. Some admissible cases may have no positive gap; the plan does not promise otherwise.
What if the LP remains as wide as the outcome-range-only bounds in a covered case?

That would not, by itself, contradict uniform coverage. It would mean the proposed restrictions and band uncertainty do not yield a certified strict improvement in that case. Validity and strict informativeness must be assessed separately.
Would strict dual tightening require the LP to select one treatment-effect value?

No. The lower and upper feasible effects can both move inward from the outcome-range-only endpoints while remaining different from each other. The confidence set would then be strictly narrower without point identification.
Is “without inversion” still an accurate description of this plan?

Yes, for the proposed construction: multinomial bands and a δ-relaxed latent-mixture LP would produce effect bounds, with dual conditions assessing narrowing. The plan does not require testing each candidate treatment effect and inverting those tests. It still requires its own coverage proof.
What would count as completing the coverage part, as opposed to merely setting up the LP?

Completion would require justified simultaneous 95% multinomial-band calibration and a proof that, uniformly over proxy strengths 0–0.2 and violations δ ≤ 0.05, band containment leads to inclusion of the true treatment effect in the LP-based set. Writing down a feasible-region optimization without that argument would leave the coverage part incomplete.
And what would complete the informativeness part?

It would require valid dual conditions whose satisfaction establishes a strict inward comparison between the LP-derived effect bounds and outcome-range-only bounds. The conditions should make clear whether they certify the lower side, the upper side, or both, while allowing the effect to remain partially identified.
So the plan’s two intended deliverables have different scopes?

Yes. The coverage deliverable is an at-least-95% uniform asymptotic guarantee across the specified proxy-strength and violation class. The dual deliverable is a characterization of cases where strict tightening occurs within the LP-based approach. Neither deliverable should be treated as automatically establishing the other.
I want to apply the 95%-band LP sets and the bounded-bridge Anderson–Rubin (AR) sets to ProxyGrid-v1, then compare minimum coverage, median confidence-set width, and endpoint exclusion.

That sets up a direct comparison of validity and informativeness on the same strength–δ grid. Minimum coverage asks about the weakest empirical coverage among the evaluated cells; median width summarizes typical set size; endpoint exclusion asks whether the sets rule out the extremes of the outcome-range-only bounds. Applying the methods and reporting those comparisons is the activity—the node does not provide the resulting numbers or a preferred method.
What should “apply both to ProxyGrid-v1” mean in this comparison?

Each method should be evaluated under the grid’s corresponding proxy-strength and δ settings, with its own stated restrictions and uncertainty treatment intact. ProxyGrid-v1 uses 10,000 Monte Carlo replications per cell at n=1,000. For an interpretable comparison, the reported coverage, width, and exclusion summaries should use clearly identified cells and consistent definitions across the two methods.
Is the 95% band itself the LP treatment-effect confidence set?

No. The simultaneous 95% multinomial bands concern observable probabilities. The LP uses those bands, together with its relaxed latent-mixture and δ-violation constraints, to produce a treatment-effect set. Its empirical coverage in ProxyGrid-v1 is what the comparison will measure; the bands’ nominal level should not be substituted for that coverage result.
And the AR set is constructed differently?

Yes. The bounded-bridge AR approach obtains its treatment-effect set through inversion of slack-adjusted proxy-moment assessments under the bridge restriction. The LP approach obtains effect bounds from optimization over band-compatible, δ-relaxed latent mixtures. The activity compares the resulting sets on the same outcomes; it does not require them to have the same construction.
Should I say explicitly what “bounded-bridge” refers to?

Yes, if you specify the restriction: |bridge| ≤ 5. It is a condition on the AR set being compared, not a proxy-strength value or a width threshold. The LP set should be described with its own actual constraints rather than assumed to inherit that restriction merely because both methods appear in one comparison.
The grid covers weak proxies and violations, correct?

Its stated settings span proxy singular values from 0 to 0.2 and δ from 0 to 0.05. Those include zero proxy strength and the upper stated violation level. The comparison should preserve those dimensions when identifying where each reported summary comes from; no particular pattern over either dimension has been given.
How would you define minimum coverage for the report?

For each method, estimate treatment-effect coverage in each evaluated strength–δ cell, then identify the smallest of those cell-level estimates over the cells included in the comparison. State which cells are included. This is a minimum over simulated cells at n=1,000, not automatically the infimum of coverage over every case in a continuous class.
Why not pool every replication and report just one coverage percentage?

Pooling can obscure a cell with relatively low coverage if other cells have higher coverage or contribute differently to the pool. A cell-level minimum keeps attention on the weakest empirical result among the evaluated settings. A pooled figure could answer another descriptive question, but it would not replace the specified minimum-coverage comparison.
Does the minimum simulated coverage prove either method meets a uniform 95% guarantee?

No. It is a finite-sample Monte Carlo summary over evaluated cells. Uniform asymptotic coverage concerns the full stated class as sample size grows, including settings between grid points and sequences approaching zero strength. The comparison can probe behavior relevant to that objective, but cannot establish the theorem from simulation alone.
What if the two minimum-coverage cells occur at different strength–δ combinations?

That would not invalidate the comparison: each method’s minimum identifies its own weakest reported cell. It would help to identify the attaining cells so a reader does not assume both minima describe the same setting. No attaining cell or minimum value is specified here.
What should “median width” summarize?

It should summarize the widths of the treatment-effect confidence sets produced by a method, with the aggregation rule stated. For example, a median can be computed within each cell and then compared across cells, or across a defined collection of replications; those answer different questions. The activity specifies median width as a comparison metric but does not choose that aggregation convention.
Would a smaller median width automatically mean a better procedure?

Not on its own. Width speaks to informativeness, while coverage indicates how often the true treatment effect is retained. The specified comparison reports both, so a width difference should be read alongside the minimum-coverage and endpoint-exclusion results rather than treated as a stand-alone verdict.
Can median width tell me whether either outcome-range endpoint was excluded?

Not necessarily. Sets can have the same width while lying in different places relative to the outcome-range bounds. Endpoint exclusion supplies that separate information. Conversely, excluding an exact endpoint does not itself establish a positive inward margin or tell us the median width.
Should endpoint exclusion distinguish the lower and upper endpoints?

That would make the comparison easier to interpret. Lower-endpoint exclusion, upper-endpoint exclusion, and exclusion of both are different events; a single combined rate may hide one-sided behavior. The activity calls for comparing endpoint exclusion but does not specify which of those summaries will be reported.
Does joint endpoint exclusion show that a set is strictly narrower than outcome-range-only bounds?

It shows that the two exact endpoint values are absent from that set. To establish positive inward margins, one must also rule out retained values arbitrarily close to those endpoints. The proposed dual analysis for the LP and the endpoint-margin analysis for AR address stronger bound comparisons than an exclusion indicator alone.
If an LP dual bound certifies narrowing, should I fold that into the endpoint-exclusion rate?

Keep the concepts distinguishable. An endpoint-exclusion rate describes what happens across simulated confidence sets. A valid dual certificate bounds an LP extreme and can establish a strict inward comparison when its conditions hold. The two may be discussed together, but the simulation rate is not itself the dual certificate, and a certificate should not be assumed from an exclusion tally.
Would the LP’s dual comparisons have to allow the same δ as the LP set being measured?

Yes. To explain the width or endpoint behavior of the 95%-band LP set, a dual bound must apply to that set’s actual simultaneous bands and permitted δ ≤ 0.05 proxy-independence violations. A bound computed after removing either allowance would describe a different optimization problem.
Should the two methods be compared on the same replications?

Using the same simulated cases and, where applicable, the same replications would make their summaries more directly comparable. The activity states that both are applied to ProxyGrid-v1, but does not spell out whether outputs are paired replication by replication. The report should make that design detail clear rather than assume it.
Could the LP have better endpoint exclusion but worse minimum coverage?

That is a possible comparison pattern, not a reported finding. It illustrates why the three outcomes should remain separate: more frequent exclusion is not automatically desirable if it accompanies inadequate coverage. The activity is meant to reveal the observed pattern rather than assume how the methods rank.
Could the methods tie on median width but differ on endpoint exclusion?

Yes, as a general possibility. A median is only one summary of set sizes, and width alone does not specify which values remain. The comparison would need the actual entries to say whether such a tie or difference occurs in ProxyGrid-v1.
How should I handle the zero-strength cells in reporting?

Keep them identifiable within the strength–δ comparison. They are included in the stated proxy-strength range and are particularly pertinent to weak-proxy behavior. A pooled median or overall exclusion figure could mask what happens there, so any zero-strength-specific conclusion should be tied to its own reported results rather than inferred from a grid-wide summary.
And the cells at δ=0.05?

They represent the upper stated violation level within the grid, subject to the specified meaning of δ. Their coverage, width, and exclusion outcomes should not be inferred from cells with smaller δ. The minimum-coverage comparison might or might not be attained there; no result has been supplied.
What is the main caution when interpreting an empirical advantage in width?

Make sure both sets address the same target and that each method’s stated restrictions are visible. A narrower set obtained under different admissibility conditions need not represent an unconditional improvement. Also retain the coverage comparison: a median-width advantage is a descriptive simulation result, not proof of valid narrowing across the full class.
Do the 10,000 replications per cell make the coverage minimum exact?

No. Each cell’s coverage estimate has Monte Carlo variation, and taking a minimum across estimated rates does not remove it. The replication count gives information for a reasonably detailed comparison, but neither the minimum nor the median is an exact population quantity merely because many replications were run.
Can I use these three comparisons to declare one approach universally preferable?

Not from the activity alone. It names the measures to compare on ProxyGrid-v1; it does not give their values or a rule for trading coverage against width and endpoint exclusion. Even reported rankings on this grid would be bounded by the evaluated settings and the conditions of each method.
What would be an accurate description of the activity before seeing results?

Apply the 95%-band LP and |bridge| ≤ 5 AR confidence sets to ProxyGrid-v1’s strength–δ cells, then compare each method’s minimum simulated treatment-effect coverage, median confidence-set width, and exclusion of the outcome-range endpoints. Report the aggregation and exclusion definitions clearly; the activity itself does not establish which method performs better.

ProxyGrid-v1’s TV-stress case at δ=0.04 caused bridge drift of 0.20. The LP covered 95.3%, while the moment-slack Anderson–Rubin (AR) approach had 0% limiting coverage. How should I report that contrast?

Keep the two coverage statements distinct: in this TV-stress case, the LP’s reported coverage was 95.3%, whereas the moment-slack AR approach had 0% limiting coverage. Why emphasize the word “limiting” for AR?

Because 0% limiting coverage describes its asymptotic behavior in the stated stress case. It should not be rewritten as a 0% coverage frequency observed in the Monte Carlo replications. The LP figure is reported as 95.3% coverage in ProxyGrid-v1; this finding does not label that figure a limiting probability.
Can I put both percentages in the same sentence?

Yes, as long as their different meanings remain visible: “At δ=0.04, ProxyGrid-v1’s TV-stress case produced bridge drift of 0.20; the LP’s reported coverage was 95.3%, while moment-slack AR had 0% limiting coverage.”
Does the finding identify why the bridge drift arose?

No. It says the TV-stress case caused bridge drift of 0.20, but gives no further mechanism or definition of that drift. You can report the amount and the setting without inferring which particular probability or moment component produced it.
Should I interpret 0.20 as the bridge’s absolute value?
Not from this finding. It reports a *drift* of 0.20, not the bridge’s level, norm, or endpoint value. Equating those quantities would add information that has not been supplied.
What does δ=0.04 specify here?
It specifies the proxy-independence violation level for this TV-stress case. The result is tied to δ=0.04; it does not give coverage outcomes at other violation levels.
Can I say the LP result was measured under zero-strength proxies?
No proxy-strength value is stated for this TV-stress finding. ProxyGrid-v1 spans strength–δ cells, but this particular result should not be assigned to a zero-strength cell without that information.
Does 95.3% describe the minimum LP coverage across the grid?
That is not stated. The 95.3% figure belongs to the reported TV-stress case at δ=0.04. The finding does not identify it as a grid-wide minimum or provide LP coverage for the other cells.
And does the AR result mean every possible AR procedure has zero limiting coverage under this kind of stress?
No. The finding names the *moment-slack AR approach* in this TV-stress case. It does not establish the behavior of every AR construction or every way of accounting for proxy-independence violations.
Would it be accurate to say the LP and AR behaved very differently here?

Yes. Reported LP coverage of 95.3% and 0% limiting coverage for moment-slack AR are sharply different outcomes in the stated case. Preserve the empirical-versus-limiting distinction when describing that difference.
Does this comparison explain whether one method produced narrower confidence sets?
No. Coverage alone does not give confidence-set width. Although the broader comparison includes width as a measure, this finding provides no median width or case-specific width for either method.
What about exclusion of the outcome-range endpoints?
That is also unreported in this finding. Neither the 95.3% coverage figure nor the 0% limiting coverage figure tells us which outcome-range endpoints the resulting sets excluded.
Can the LP’s 95.3% be presented as a uniform coverage proof?
No. It is a reported coverage outcome for the TV-stress case. A result at δ=0.04 does not by itself establish coverage uniformly over other strengths, violation levels, or stress cases.
Does the 0% limiting figure tell us what AR coverage was at n=1,000?
No. A limiting coverage statement does not specify the coverage frequency at a particular finite sample size. The finding gives no separate finite-sample AR percentage for this TV-stress case.
Should I attribute the entire difference in coverage to the drift of 0.20?

The finding connects the TV stress with bridge drift of 0.20 and reports the contrasting coverage outcomes. It does not isolate the drift as the sole cause of their difference or quantify how coverage would change at another drift magnitude. Reporting the association is more precise than asserting a decomposition that was not supplied.
Could I say that the LP handled every permitted proxy-independence violation because it covered 95.3% here?
No. This result concerns the stated TV-stress case at δ=0.04. It does not report outcomes for every violation magnitude or every form of departure within an allowed class.
Is it important to retain the label “TV-stress” in a short report?

Yes. It identifies the setting to which the bridge drift and coverage figures belong. Without it, a reader might mistake the two numbers for overall ProxyGrid-v1 summaries rather than results for this particular stress case.
What is the most defensible concise takeaway?

In ProxyGrid-v1’s TV-stress case at δ=0.04, bridge drift was 0.20; the LP had reported coverage of 95.3%, while moment-slack AR had 0% *limiting* coverage. The finding makes a strong case-specific coverage contrast but supplies no width, endpoint-exclusion, or grid-wide coverage result.

I’ve decided to adopt the LP approach for TV-bounded proxy-independence violations. I’ll retain the proved Anderson–Rubin (AR) coverage claim only when δ is defined in moment space or the TV slack is adjusted for the bridge.

That draws a boundary between two ways of quantifying the allowed violation. The LP is the adopted approach for TV-bounded violations. The AR coverage claim is restricted to moment-space δ or to TV slack that accounts for the bridge; it should not be stated for an unadjusted TV allowance.
Why does it matter whether δ is a TV bound or a moment-space bound?

They constrain different quantities. A moment-space bound directly limits the discrepancy relevant to the proxy moments. A TV bound limits a distributional departure; its effect on a bridge-weighted moment needs to be accounted for. Using the same numerical δ as moment slack without that connection could understate the permitted moment discrepancy.
So for TV-bounded violations, is the decision to stop using AR entirely?

No. The decision adopts LP for TV-bounded violations, but it also names bridge-adjusted TV slack as a condition under which the AR coverage claim may be retained. The restriction is on what can support that claim, not a blanket statement that AR can never be used with TV-bounded violations.
What does “bridge-adjusted TV slack” mean at this level of detail?

It means the allowance in the AR moments must reflect how a permitted TV departure can affect moments involving the bridge. The decision does not specify a conversion formula or a new critical value, so it would be premature to assign a numerical adjustment. The essential point is that TV δ cannot simply be treated as moment-space δ without accounting for the bridge.
Does a bound such as |bridge| ≤ 5 make the two δ definitions identical?

No. A bridge bound can help control how a TV violation translates into a moment discrepancy, but it does not make TV distance and moment-space discrepancy the same quantity. The conversion still needs to be justified for the moments in use. The number 5 should not silently be substituted for that argument.
Can I continue saying that the AR procedure has uniform 95% coverage for every violation labeled δ ≤ 0.05?

Not without stating what δ measures. The decision retains the proved AR coverage claim only for moment-space δ or bridge-adjusted TV slack. Writing merely “δ ≤ 0.05” for a TV-bounded class could imply that unadjusted moment slack suffices, which is outside the decision’s stated scope.
Should the LP be described as a 95% uniform coverage theorem now that it is adopted for TV-bounded violations?

Adoption alone does not establish that theorem. You can say the LP is the chosen approach for TV-bounded violations. Any claim of at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage for it still needs to be supported under the specified TV class, proxy-strength range, band calibration, and LP containment conditions.
Does this decision choose the LP because its sets are always narrower?

No such universal width comparison is part of the decision. The choice identifies the approach for TV-bounded violations. Whether its confidence sets strictly improve on outcome-range-only bounds remains a separate question for the relevant dual bounds and conditions.
How should I phrase the scope of the AR statement when δ is in moment space?

Say explicitly that the violation allowance is measured in the proxy-moment space used by the AR inversion, and retain the other conditions of the proved coverage claim. The decision does not authorize turning that claim into coverage for every form of proxy-independence departure that happens to be assigned the same numerical δ.
And if I want to discuss AR under a TV bound?

Make the bridge adjustment explicit as a condition of the coverage statement. In particular, distinguish the TV bound itself from the slack actually allowed in the AR moment assessment. The decision does not supply the adjustment’s formula, so it should not be represented as an unqualified, already specified construction.
Are the moment-space and bridge-adjusted TV cases alternative routes, or must both conditions hold at once?

The decision states them as alternatives for retaining the AR coverage claim: δ is specified in moment space, *or* a TV-bounded violation is translated into bridge-adjusted slack. In either case, the coverage claim must retain its other applicable conditions; the word “or” does not remove them.
Does adopting LP for TV-bounded violations mean treating proxy independence as exact in its constraints?
No. The LP route for TV-bounded violations needs to permit the violations within the stated TV class. Adoption of LP is not a decision to set the allowed departure to zero.
Would simultaneous 95% multinomial bands alone justify that LP coverage claim?

Not alone. The bands address joint uncertainty in the observable probabilities. For the treatment-effect set to inherit coverage, the LP relaxation must also retain the true effect when those probabilities are covered and the permitted TV-bounded violations are present. The decision to use LP does not bypass that containment requirement.
Is the coverage distinction related to point identification?

No. It concerns whether the allowed violations are translated into the restrictions used by the inference procedure. Either approach can produce a non-singleton treatment-effect set. Coverage and possible narrowing can be discussed without asserting point identification.
Could I present the decision as saying the proved AR result is false under every TV-bounded violation?

That would be too broad. The decision specifically permits retaining the AR coverage claim with bridge-adjusted TV slack. It rules out extending the claim to an unadjusted TV interpretation merely by relabeling moment-space δ; it does not rule out every AR treatment of TV-bounded violations.
What is a concise statement that preserves the decision and its limits?

Adopt the LP approach for TV-bounded proxy-independence violations. Retain the proved AR coverage claim only when δ is a moment-space allowance or TV violations are accommodated by bridge-adjusted slack; do not extend either approach’s coverage or tightening claims beyond its stated conditions.

I want to implement the LP-primary, AR-moment-only policy. The next tasks are to prove 95% uniform coverage for the LP under TV-bounded violations δ ≤ 0.05 and proxy strengths 0–0.2, and to derive dual certificates for strict tightening.

That gives the LP the primary role for the TV-bounded class, while the AR component of this implementation is confined to moment-space violations. The LP coverage proof must address the full stated range, including zero proxy strength and violations through δ=0.05. The dual certificates are a separate deliverable: they should establish when the LP-based treatment-effect set is strictly narrower than outcome-range-only bounds. Neither deliverable is completed by stating the activity.
What does “LP-primary” commit this implementation to?

It means the LP-based confidence set is the principal procedure for the stated TV-bounded violation class. It does not mean that LP coverage or strict tightening has already been proved. The proof and dual-certificate work are precisely what this activity calls for.
And how should I understand “AR-moment-only” here?

It describes the AR component of this implementation: its violation allowance is expressed in the moment space used by that procedure, rather than treating a TV bound as though it were automatically the same amount of moment slack. It should not be read as a new theorem about all possible AR procedures.
Can I call both allowances δ as long as each is at most 0.05?

Only if their meanings remain explicit. For the LP coverage task, δ ≤ 0.05 is a TV bound on the permitted proxy-independence violation. For the AR component of this implementation, the allowance is in moment space. Giving them the same symbol and numerical limit would not make the two measures interchangeable.
Does the LP proof require treating conditional independence as exact?

No. Its stated target includes TV-bounded violations up to δ=0.05. The LP constraints and the coverage argument must admit the true treatment effect when such a permitted violation is present. A proof confined to exact proxy independence would establish a narrower claim than the one planned.
What should the uniform coverage statement look like?

For an LP-based confidence set C_n and true treatment effect τ(P), the intended asymptotic statement is that the limit inferior, as sample size grows, of the infimum over the stated TV-violation and proxy-strength class of Pr_P{τ(P) ∈ C_n} is at least 0.95. The class must be defined precisely enough for that infimum to have a clear meaning. This is the claim to prove, not a result already supplied by the policy.
Why does the strength range 0–0.2 matter to the proof?

Zero belongs to that range, so the proof cannot rely on a positive lower bound on proxy strength. Uniformity also has to address admissible cases whose strength approaches zero as sample size grows, not merely fixed positive strengths considered one at a time. The number 0.2 is the stated upper end of the coverage class, not a treatment-effect bound.
Does the proof have to cover δ=0.05 itself?

Yes. The condition is δ ≤ 0.05, so its boundary is included. The proof must also cover other permitted violation levels, rather than assume without argument that checking only the boundary settles the entire class.
What role do the simultaneous 95% multinomial bands play in this LP route?

They are the proposed means of accounting for joint uncertainty in the observable multinomial probabilities used by the latent-mixture LP. To obtain treatment-effect coverage, the proof must connect joint band containment to feasibility of the true effect under the TV-relaxed LP constraints. A nominal 95% label on the bands does not, by itself, prove uniform 95% coverage for the resulting effect set.
What is the critical direction of that LP containment argument?

When the simultaneous bands contain the true observable probabilities, an admissible case in the TV-bounded class must remain represented within the LP relaxation, with its true treatment effect among the resulting feasible effect values. The relaxation may admit extra values; for coverage, it must not exclude the true one. Establishing that implication uniformly is part of the planned proof.
If the LP is relaxed enough to contain the truth, is the 95% proof finished?

Not necessarily. The argument also needs appropriately calibrated joint bands and a uniform link between their containment event and effect-set containment over the stated class. A relaxation that contains the truth but is combined with bands lacking the required coverage would not establish the planned 95% result.
Should I claim finite-sample 95% coverage?

The stated goal is at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage. This activity does not specify a finite-sample coverage theorem, so the proof target should not be silently strengthened to one. The numerical 95% is a coverage lower bound to establish under the stated asymptotic and uniform qualifications.
Does LP-primary mean I can import the AR bridge condition |bridge| ≤ 5 into the LP proof?

No bridge restriction is specified for this LP coverage task. The LP proof should state the conditions it actually uses rather than inherit |bridge| ≤ 5 merely because the two procedures are discussed in one policy. Likewise, any conclusion obtained under an added restriction would need to retain that restriction in its scope.
How does the policy prevent confusion about TV slack in the AR comparison?

By making the implemented AR component moment-only, it avoids treating a TV violation magnitude as an unadjusted proxy-moment allowance. The LP takes the primary role for TV-bounded violations. That division clarifies what each procedure is meant to cover; it does not itself prove either procedure’s performance.
Does that mean a bridge-adjusted treatment of TV violations is mathematically impossible for AR?

No. The description of this implementation is AR-moment-only; it is not a claim that every other AR formulation is impossible. The activity asks for an LP coverage proof for TV-bounded violations and keeps the AR component’s violation scale in moment space.
What should a dual certificate demonstrate?

It should give a valid bound on an LP treatment-effect extreme that lies strictly inward from the corresponding outcome-range-only endpoint. An upper-side certificate would place the largest feasible effect below the range-only upper bound; a lower-side certificate would place the smallest feasible effect above the range-only lower bound. Those comparisons certify informativeness without requiring a uniquely identified effect.
Do I need a certificate for both sides to call the set strictly narrower?

A valid strict inward comparison on one side can demonstrate a one-sided improvement, provided the resulting set is compared appropriately with the outcome-range-only bounds. If the intended claim is tightening at both endpoints, each side needs its own supporting comparison. The derivation should specify which conclusion its certificates warrant.
Must the dual certificate use the TV-relaxed constraints and the multinomial bands?

Yes, if it is to certify narrowing of the same LP-based confidence set whose coverage is being proved. A certificate for an LP that assumes exact independence or treats the observed probabilities as known exactly would concern a different feasible set. The proposed dual conditions need to remain valid with the permitted TV violations and band uncertainty included.
Could a dual bound equal to the outcome-range-only endpoint count as a certificate of tightening?

It could be a valid bound, but equality supplies no strict inward gap at that endpoint. A certificate of strict tightening needs a positive difference from the relevant outcome-range-only endpoint. The activity does not assert that such a difference exists throughout the coverage class.
Why not infer tightening directly from the uniform coverage proof?

Coverage and tightening answer different questions. Coverage asks whether the true effect remains in the set at the required rate; tightening asks whether values allowed by the outcome range alone are excluded. An LP can be valid but as wide as those range-only bounds. That is why dual certificates are a distinct part of the activity.
Could a dual certificate establish narrowing even if the effect remains partially identified?

Yes. The certified lower and upper effect bounds can be strictly more restrictive than outcome-range-only bounds while still enclosing multiple possible effects. The activity seeks conditions for that strict improvement, not a proof of point identification.
What should I avoid claiming if I find a certificate in just one strength–δ case?

Do not generalize that certificate to every strength from 0 to 0.2 or every TV violation δ ≤ 0.05 without an argument that covers them. The coverage claim is intended to be uniform over the class; strict narrowing is to be characterized under the conditions where the dual comparison holds.
Could the LP have uniform coverage even at zero strength but no dual narrowing certificate there?

Yes. Inclusion of zero strength in the proposed coverage class does not promise that the restrictions remain informative enough to tighten the bounds at zero. Validity of the set and a positive dual gap are separate properties, including at that boundary.
What would count as completing this activity?

Implement the stated division between an LP-primary procedure for TV-bounded violations and an AR component using moment-space allowances; establish at least 95% uniform asymptotic coverage for the LP over proxy strengths 0–0.2 and TV δ ≤ 0.05; and derive valid dual conditions that certify strict improvement over outcome-range-only bounds when they hold. The coverage theorem and the dual certificates should each state their own conditions and conclusions.

ProxyLP-v1 is ready. It documents the LP-primary and AR-moment-only rules, uniform 95% LP coverage for TV-bounded proxy-independence violations δ ≤ 0.05 and proxy strengths 0–0.2, and dual certificates for tightening treatment-effect bounds. How should I describe what the artifact establishes?

Describe three parts, keeping their scopes separate. ProxyLP-v1 makes the LP the primary approach for TV-bounded violations and confines its AR rule to moment-space allowances. Because they are not interchangeable descriptions of δ. A TV bound concerns a distributional departure, whereas a moment-space allowance concerns the discrepancies used by AR. ProxyLP-v1’s LP coverage claim is for TV δ ≤ 0.05; its AR-moment-only rule should not be described as granting that same TV coverage merely because both discussions use the symbol δ.

It is described as *uniform* coverage over the stated class: proxy strengths from 0 to 0.2 and TV violations δ ≤ 0.05. That is broader than reporting coverage at selected cells. State the range and the TV interpretation of δ whenever you present the claim.
Does the 0–0.2 interval include zero-strength proxies?

Yes. Zero is included in 0–0.2, so the documented uniform LP coverage result encompasses zero-strength cases within its stated class. That does not mean every such case yields a narrow confidence set.
And δ=0.05 itself is included?
Yes. δ ≤ 0.05 includes the boundary value 0.05. The coverage statement should not be quietly narrowed to exact proxy independence or to violations strictly below 0.05.
Can I describe the result as finite-sample 95% coverage?

ProxyLP-v1’s description says uniform 95% LP coverage, but does not specify a finite-sample guarantee. In the setting of the stated coverage goal, describe it as a uniform asymptotic coverage result unless the artifact explicitly supplies a stronger finite-sample claim. Do not infer finite-sample validity from the number 95%.
Should I say coverage equals 95% across the class?

No. A 95% coverage guarantee is a lower-bound claim, not an assertion that every admissible case has exactly 95% coverage. “At least 95% uniformly over the stated class” expresses the intended guarantee without implying equality.
Does the coverage result identify the true treatment effect as a single number?

No. It concerns whether the LP-based set contains the true treatment effect at the stated rate. The set may contain multiple values. Coverage of a treatment-effect confidence set does not require point identification.
Where do the dual certificates fit if coverage is already documented?

They address informativeness rather than coverage. A dual certificate can bound an LP treatment-effect extreme strictly inside the corresponding outcome-range-only endpoint, establishing a narrower bound when its conditions hold. The coverage statement says the set remains valid over its specified class; it does not tell you which cases admit a strict dual comparison.
Does saying ProxyLP-v1 has dual tightening certificates mean it proves every LP set is narrower?

No. The certificates provide conditions for certifying tightening. Without a statement that those conditions hold throughout the coverage class, their existence should not be turned into a universal narrowing claim. The LP set can be covered by the uniform validity result even where a strict certificate is unavailable.
What is a useful way to describe a certificate at one endpoint?

Conceptually, a certificate for the upper endpoint places a valid upper bound on the LP-feasible treatment effects strictly below the outcome-range-only upper bound. A lower-endpoint certificate analogously places a lower bound strictly above the range-only lower bound.
